title: What is truth? (John 18:28–38)
hook: Pilate asks and doesn't wait for an answer
carry: I find in him no fault at all

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter at the anthrakia, the charcoal fire, saying I am not. Your line was warming himself. Where did you step out of the crowd? Day six hundred forty-four.

Out, in, out again. In today's scene Pilate can't stay in one place. The priests who bring Jesus won't go into the governor's hall, John says, so they can keep themselves ready to eat the Passover. So Pilate goes out to them, then back in to the prisoner, then out again. Watch his feet as the morning goes on. And in the middle of all that coming and going, he asks a question as large as any in the Gospel, then heads for the door.

It's early morning. Jesus is brought to the Roman governor's headquarters. Pilate is the man who will soon say he has power to crucify, and the conversation shuttles back and forth between him and the prisoner. Pilate asks: are you a king? And Jesus answers, in the King James Bible, "My kingdom is not of this world." Then he says what he came for: "To this end was I born, and for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth. Every one that is of the truth heareth my voice." And Pilate says three words: "What is truth?" And then, John tells us, he went out again. He asks the biggest question in the room and walks away before anyone can answer. Four hundred years ago the English writer Francis Bacon opened an essay with this scene: "What is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer." Was he jesting? Nobody knows his tone. Readers have heard it as sneering, as weary, as a politician who's heard too many sincere men. The Greek word for truth is aletheia, and in John it's more than correct information. Jesus has already said, I am the way, the truth, and the life. So in John's telling, Pilate asks what truth is while Truth is standing in front of him. The irony is the point. Then Pilate goes out and tells them, I find in him no fault at all. Let's look back. This week: courage in trouble, the hour, keep them, be one, the garden, the fire, and now a question left hanging.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`
`BORN TO BEAR WITNESS TO THE TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: wait for an answer today. Settle, and breathe. Think of a question you've been asking without really waiting for the answer. How are you doing, said in passing. What do you think, said while already reaching for your phone. Maybe a question you ask God, or yourself, and then change the subject. Pick one. For these minutes, ask it again, slowly, and then don't move on. Just wait. If you pray, you can ask it in prayer and leave a silence afterward. The bell holds the time.
Pilate. The Roman governor who asked, what is truth, and walked out of the room before anyone could answer.
Your line: I find in him no fault at all. Today, ask someone one real question, and then stay for the answer, all of it. Day six hundred forty-four, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians read Jesus's trial before Pilate during Holy Week, and churches that say the Apostles' Creed name him in it: suffered under Pontius Pilate.

original.note: Greek: what is truth? aletheia, truth; in John, more than correct facts: something you can be 'of'.

trapdoor: what you thought: Pilate asks a philosophy question.
what it means: the man with the power in the room asks what truth is, and walks out before the answer.
what a scholar hears: the irony John sets up ('I am the truth', 14:6), and Pilate's restless shuttling, out to the accusers and in to the prisoner (18:29–38), staging the question.
recall: see how they love one another
